task_title: VFR Weather Minimums, Special VFR and Cruising Altitudes
area: Area III. Airspace and VFR Rules
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state the 91.155 visibility and cloud clearance for any airspace class, altitude and time of day, say when a surface area needs special VFR and what 91.157 requires, and pick the right 91.159 cruising altitude.
why: Most VFR weather violations and many fatal accidents start with a pilot who was a little below the minimums and kept going. Knowing the exact numbers lets you see the line before you cross it.

prereading.what: The rules themselves: the basic VFR weather minimums table, the surface area rules, special VFR and VFR cruising altitudes.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.155 to 91.159

prereading.what: Overlapping airspace, TBL 3-1-1 Basic VFR Weather Minimums and TBL 3-1-2 VFR Cruising Altitudes.
prereading.label: AIM 3-1-3 to 3-1-5

prereading.what: Special VFR clearances: who to ask, what the clearance says, where it ends, and the night rule.
prereading.label: AIM 4-4-6

prereading.what: Class D and Class E surface areas, part-time towers and surface area extensions.
prereading.label: AIM 3-2-5 to 3-2-6

prereading.what: Basic VFR weather minimums with the color chart in Figure 15-8.
prereading.label: PHAK 15-7 to 15-8

prereading.what: Inadvertent VFR flight into IMC: recognition, keeping control, turns, climbs and descents.
prereading.label: AFH 18-17 to 18-21

warmup: You are at 1,000 ft AGL in Class G at dusk with 2 miles of visibility, clear of clouds. Ten minutes later it is legally night. What changes, and are you still legal?

key_terms.def: Average forward horizontal distance you can see and identify prominent objects from the cockpit in flight.
Prevailing horizontal visibility near the surface, reported by the National Weather Service or an accredited observer.
Height above the surface of the lowest layer reported broken, overcast or obscuration (not thin or partial).
From the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
Class B, C, D or E controlled airspace that starts at the surface for an airport.
ATC clearance to fly VFR in a surface area below basic VFR minimums: clear of clouds, 1 SM visibility.
Odd or even thousands plus 500 ft by magnetic course, when more than 3,000 ft above the surface.
Your ground track measured from magnetic north. It, not heading, picks the cruising altitude.
Trying to keep sight of the ground at low altitude while instrument conditions exist.
Marginal VFR: ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft and/or visibility 3 to 5 miles.

chunks.title: Reading 91.155: the words that decide it

body.p: 91.155(a) says no person may fly VFR when the flight visibility, or the distance from clouds, is less than the table shows for that altitude and class of airspace [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. Every answer depends on four defined words, so get them exact.

head: Term
What 14 CFR 1.1 says
Why it matters
rows: Average forward horizontal distance from the cockpit in flight at which prominent objects can be seen and identified [[60:7|14 CFR 1.1 Flight visibility]]
This is the number in the 91.155 table. It is your judgment in the air.
Prevailing visibility near the surface reported by the NWS or an accredited observer [[60:8|14 CFR 1.1 Ground visibility]]
Used for takeoff, landing and pattern entry in surface areas, 91.155(d) [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]]
Lowest layer reported broken, overcast or obscuration, not thin or partial [[60:3|14 CFR 1.1 Ceiling]]
A FEW or SCT layer is not a ceiling.
End of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1 Night]]
Sets the day or night line in Class G.

body.p: Where airspace overlaps, the more restrictive class's rules apply [[33:175|AIM 3-1-3]]. At the base altitude of a Class E area, you count as being in the airspace below it [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]]. So at exactly 1,200 ft AGL under a 1,200-ft Class E floor, Class G minimums still apply.

callout.text: Read each cloud clearance as a box around the airplane: how far below the cloud, how far above it, and how far beside it. Then check visibility separately.

check.q: METAR: FEW008 SCT015 BKN035 OVC060. What is the ceiling?
check.a: 3,500 ft. The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer; FEW and SCT layers don't count [[60:3|14 CFR 1.1 Ceiling]].

chunks.title: Classes A to E: the basic VFR minimums

head: Airspace
Flight visibility
Distance from clouds
rows: 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
Class E at or above 10,000 MSL
1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]

body.p: Class A is "not applicable" because you can't fly VFR there. From 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL 600, all flights are IFR unless otherwise authorized [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]. Class B is the only class with a plain "clear of clouds" rule, because everyone in it has an ATC clearance and gets separation [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]].

callout.text: "3-152": 3 SM, 1,000 above, 500 below, 2,000 beside. It covers C, D and E below 10,000. At 10,000 MSL and up it becomes "5-111": 5 SM, 1,000 above, 1,000 below, 1 SM beside [[33:176|AIM 3-1-4]].
Common mistake: the 10,000-ft line is MSL, not AGL. A pilot at 10,500 MSL over 6,000-ft terrain needs 5 SM in Class E even though he is only 4,500 ft above the ground [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

check.q: You will cruise at 8,500 ft MSL in Class E. Clouds are above you. What visibility and how far below the clouds?
check.a: 3 SM visibility and at least 500 ft below the clouds (plus 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal) [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

chunks.title: Class G: the 1,200-foot line and day versus night

body.p: Class G is the airspace not designated A, B, C, D or E [[33:189|AIM 3-3-1]]. Its minimums change with height above the surface, MSL altitude and time of day [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

head: Class G altitude
Day
Night
rows: 1,200 ft or less above the surface (any MSL altitude)
More than 1,200 ft AGL, below 10,000 MSL
More than 1,200 ft AGL and at or above 10,000 MSL
5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]

callout.text: 91.155(b)(2): at night in Class G below 1,200 ft AGL, if the visibility is less than 3 SM but not less than 1 SM, you may fly an airplane clear of clouds in an airport traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)]].

body.p: In practice, Class G is mostly low. Class E transition areas around airports with instrument procedures start at 700 or 1,200 ft AGL, and federal airways start at 1,200 ft AGL [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]]. Class G generally extends up to 14,500 MSL; at and above that it is Class E, except within 1,500 ft of the terrain [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]]. The low Class G is where the "1 SM, clear of clouds" rule lives, and it is also where terrain and towers are closest.

callout.text: Common mistake: "day" here ends at the end of evening civil twilight, not at sunset, because that is when night begins under 14 CFR 1.1 [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1 Night]]. Special VFR uses a different line: sunset. See the special VFR chunk.

check.q: Night, Class G, 900 ft AGL, 2 SM visibility, on downwind 1/4 mile from the runway. Legal?
check.a: Yes. 91.155(b)(2) allows clear of clouds with at least 1 SM in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)]].

body.p: Inside the lateral limits of a surface area (Class B, C, D or E airspace that starts at the surface for an airport), 91.155 adds two rules on top of the table:

bullets: Ceiling: no VFR beneath the ceiling when the ceiling is less than 1,000 ft, except under special VFR [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]].

Visibility: no VFR takeoff, landing or entering the traffic pattern unless ground visibility at that airport is at least 3 SM. If ground visibility isn't reported, flight visibility in the takeoff, landing or pattern must be at least 3 SM [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].

body.p: On the sectional, Class D airspace is a blue dashed line [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]] and a Class E surface area is a magenta dashed line [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]]. A Class E surface area needs weather reporting at the airport and radio coverage down to the runway [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6e]]. Class E extensions that start at the surface become part of the surface area while it is in effect [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].

Part-time towers matter. When a Class D tower closes, the surface area may become Class E or Class G [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]]. If it becomes Class G, the 1,000-and-3 rules no longer apply there, and the Class G table does.

callout.text: Changed: the old "A/FD" (Airport/Facility Directory) is now the Chart Supplement [[1:27|PHAK 1-12]]. It is where the airport entry says "other times Class E" or "other times Class G" [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

Common mistake: 91.155(c) bans VFR beneath a ceiling under 1,000 ft. It does not ban flying over the surface area above the clouds, as long as you meet the cloud clearance for that class [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]].

check.q: A towered Class D airport reports ceiling 1,500 OVC and visibility 2 SM. Can you land VFR?
check.a: No. The ceiling is fine, but VFR takeoff, landing or pattern entry needs 3 SM ground visibility [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]]. You need special VFR or IFR.

body.p: Special VFR replaces the 91.155 minimums below 10,000 ft MSL, inside the upward extension of the lateral limits of a surface area [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(a)]]. Outside that airspace it doesn't exist.

head: 91.157 requirement
Airplane rule
rows: Flight visibility at least 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]
Ground visibility at least 1 SM; if not reported, flight visibility at least 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]]
Sunrise to sunset, unless the pilot meets the part 61 instrument flight requirements and the airplane is equipped for IFR under 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking SVFR takeoff always needs reported weather. If ground visibility isn't reported, flight visibility must be at least 1 SM, and for a part 91 flight at a satellite airport with no weather reporting, "flight visibility" includes what you see from the cockpit in takeoff position [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]]. Your estimate is not an official weather or ground visibility report [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(d)]].
Common mistake: night for SVFR starts at sunset, not at the end of civil twilight. 91.157(b)(4) says "between sunrise and sunset" [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

body.p: Some busy airports ban fixed-wing SVFR. They are listed in Part 91 Appendix D, Section 3 (for example Atlanta, Boston, Chicago O'Hare, LaGuardia and JFK) [[60:648|14 CFR Part 91 App. D, Sec. 3]] [[60:649|14 CFR Part 91 App. D, Sec. 3]], and the sectional prints "NO SVFR" above the airport name [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]].

check.q: Sunset is 1812. Civil twilight ends 1838. You are a private pilot without an instrument rating. Latest time you may fly fixed-wing SVFR?
check.a: 1812, sunset. SVFR for airplanes is between sunrise and sunset unless the pilot meets the instrument requirements and the airplane is IFR-equipped [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

chunks.title: Special VFR in practice: asking and flying

body.p: You need a clearance before operating in a Class B, C, D or E surface area when the weather is below VFR. ATC gives SVFR traffic permitting, and only if it won't delay IFR traffic [[33:277|AIM 4-4-6a]].

head: Question
AIM 4-4-6 answer
rows: The tower if there is one in the surface area. In a Class E surface area, the nearest tower, FSS or center [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]
Not needed. State your intentions in enough detail [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]
None assigned, because you must stay clear of clouds. ATC may say "at or below" an altitude for traffic [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]
You are responsible for obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]
ATC separates SVFR flights from each other and from IFR flights, only inside the surface area [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]
Departing a nontowered airport inside the surface area?
Monitor ASOS or AWOS, tell the controller you have the "one-minute weather", and state intentions [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]

callout.text: Once you leave the surface area, the clearance ends and so does ATC separation [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. You are back under 91.155, so make sure the weather outside meets the table for that airspace.

Common mistake: misquoting the night SVFR rule. 91.157(b)(4) says the person getting the clearance must meet "the applicable requirements for instrument flight under part 61," and the aircraft must be equipped as required in 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]. AIM 4-4-6g says it more simply: the pilot is instrument rated and the aircraft is equipped for IFR flight [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. Neither text names 61.57(c) recency. Reading the rule to include it is an interpretation, not the rule's words. Being IFR current under 61.57(c) [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] meets either reading.

check.q: You get SVFR out of a Class D surface area. Three miles past the boundary, does ATC still separate you from IFR traffic?
check.a: No. SVFR clearances are effective only within the surface area, and ATC doesn't separate you after you leave it [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

body.p: In level cruising flight more than 3,000 ft above the surface, VFR pilots must fly the altitude set by magnetic course, unless ATC authorizes otherwise. It doesn't apply while holding in a pattern of 2 minutes or less, or while turning [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]].

Above 18,000 ft MSL, maintain the altitude or flight level assigned by ATC [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(b)]]. AIM TBL 3-1-2 also lists VFR flight levels from FL 185 to FL 290 [[33:177|AIM 3-1-5, TBL 3-1-2]], but Class A starts at 18,000 MSL and is IFR unless otherwise authorized [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]. For a normal VFR flight, that column has no use.

callout.text: Common mistake: the rule uses magnetic course (ground track), not heading and not true course [[33:177|AIM 3-1-5, TBL 3-1-2]]. Work from true course: west variation adds, east subtracts [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].
Common mistake: "3,000 ft" is above the surface, not MSL. Over 5,000-ft terrain, 7,500 MSL is only 2,500 AGL, so 91.159 doesn't apply yet [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]].
East is odd, west is even: "Odd people fly east." Then add 500. Compare IFR in Class G: odd or even thousands with no 500 [[33:189|AIM 3-3-3, TBL 3-3-1]].

check.q: True course 172°, variation 12° W, more than 3,000 ft AGL. Odd or even + 500?
check.a: Magnetic course is 184° (west adds) [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]], so even thousands + 500, such as 4,500 or 6,500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: is this VFR flight legal?

body.p: Run the same six questions for any point on the route, before the flight and again whenever the weather changes. 91.103 requires weather reports and forecasts for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

bullets: 1. Where am I? Class of airspace, MSL altitude, and height above the surface. At a Class E floor, use the airspace below [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]]. Where classes overlap, use the more restrictive [[33:175|AIM 3-1-3]].
2. Day or night? For 91.155, night begins at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1 Night]]. For SVFR, the line is sunset [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].
3. Do visibility and cloud clearance meet the table? [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
4. Inside a surface area? Ceiling at least 1,000 ft to fly beneath it, and 3 SM ground visibility to take off, land or enter the pattern [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].

5. If not, is there a legal option? SVFR (clearance, clear of clouds, 1 SM, and sunrise to sunset unless instrument qualified and IFR-equipped) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]], a different altitude, a delay, or IFR.
6. Cruising more than 3,000 ft AGL? Pick odd or even + 500 by magnetic course [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]].

head: Example
Answer
rows: Day, Class G, 1,000 AGL, 1.5 SM, clear of clouds
Legal: 1 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
Day, Class E, 6,500 MSL, 4 SM, 300 ft below a cloud deck
Not legal: need 500 ft below [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
Not legal: need 5 SM at or above 10,000 MSL [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]
Class D, METAR 700 OVC 3 SM, want to depart
Not VFR: ceiling below 1,000. Ask for SVFR or file IFR [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]

callout.text: Legal is the floor, not the goal. The PHAK separates what is "legal" from what is "smart" or "safe" for your experience, and suggests personal minimums for weather [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

check.q: Day, Class G, 2,000 ft AGL, 3,000 MSL, visibility 1.5 SM, cloud base 400 ft above you. Legal?
check.a: No. Visibility is fine (1 SM), but above 1,200 AGL you need 500 ft below clouds, and you have only 400 [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

chunks.title: Risk: continuing VFR into deteriorating weather

body.p: Loss of control in flight and controlled flight into terrain are two of the top four causes of fatal GA accidents. The RMH lists continued VFR into IMC as a typical path to loss of control, and says CFIT often comes from continued VFR into low ceilings or visibility [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. It "continues to cause accidents" [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

head: Pitfall
What it looks like
rows: Fixation on the destination and no thought of alternatives [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]
Trying to keep the ground in sight at low altitude while instrument conditions exist [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]
Spatial disorientation or hitting terrain; worse if not instrument rated or current [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]

body.p: Before the flight, AC 91-92 says: don't plan flights beyond your personal minimums, and don't continue VFR into IMC; wait it out or turn around if en route weather drops below your limits. Areas between reporting stations may be below VFR even when the stations are near VFR minimums, and fog may form when the temperature-dewpoint spread is 3 °C or less [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. Don't go "on top" hoping for a hole at the other end [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

**If you get caught.** The AFH says untrained pilots, or pilots whose instrument skills have eroded, lose control in about 10 minutes once they must rely on instruments alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Its first steps are recognition, keeping control, and getting help [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]:

bullets: Recognize it: if you can't hold attitude by the natural horizon, treat it as IMC and a genuine emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Trust the instruments and keep the wings level. Trim for hands-off level flight and use fingertip pressure [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

Turns: no more than 10° of bank [[24:368|AFH 18-19]]. Climbs: no more than one bar width up; descents: no more than 500 fpm [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Avoid combined maneuvers, and ask ATC to slow down if needed [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

Get help: call ATC with your problem and request; if you can't reach anyone, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. In an emergency, you may deviate from any rule to the extent needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]].

callout.text: Personal minimums beat legal minimums. MVFR (ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft or visibility 3 to 5 miles) is legal VFR in most airspace [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]], but it leaves little room when the weather is worse than forecast. Have alternatives and be ready to divert [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

check.q: Ahead the ridge disappears into cloud and the visibility is dropping. What is the safest choice?
check.a: Turn back toward the better weather before you lose visual references. Don't continue VFR into IMC; wait it out or turn around [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. Scud running under it is a known pitfall [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

bullets: Using 1 SM and clear of clouds in Class G at night. That is day only; night needs 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000 except the pattern rule [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].
Treating 10,000 ft as AGL. The 5 SM rule starts at 10,000 MSL [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].
Calling a scattered layer a ceiling [[60:3|14 CFR 1.1 Ceiling]].
Landing VFR in a Class D with 2 SM because the ceiling is high. The 3 SM ground visibility rule still applies [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].
Asking for SVFR at night without the instrument qualifications and an IFR-equipped airplane, or using civil twilight instead of sunset [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].
Expecting ATC separation after leaving the surface area on SVFR [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].
Choosing cruising altitude by heading, or applying 91.159 below 3,000 ft AGL [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]] [[33:177|AIM 3-1-5, TBL 3-1-2]].
Pressing on under lowering clouds instead of turning around early [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

check.q: Why can't you rely on "it's still light out" for SVFR without an instrument rating?
check.a: Because the SVFR time limit is sunset, not the end of civil twilight [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

scenario.title: Lowering clouds on the way to a Class D
scenario.setup: It is 1400 on a fall day. You hold a private certificate with an instrument rating, but you have not flown an approach in 9 months, so you are not instrument current. You are VFR at 5,500 ft MSL on a magnetic course of 075°, over terrain about 1,000 ft MSL, in Class E. Ahead the cloud base is lowering: a broken layer at about 4,000 ft MSL. Your destination is a towered Class D airport 40 NM ahead now reporting 1,500 broken, visibility 2 SM in mist. Sunset is 1745.

questions.q: Is 5,500 ft the right cruising altitude, and what happens to 91.159 if you descend to 3,500 ft?
questions.a: Yes. Magnetic course 075° is 0° to 179°, so odd thousands + 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. At 3,500 MSL you are only 2,500 ft above the 1,000-ft terrain, so 91.159 no longer applies; it covers only level cruise more than 3,000 ft above the surface [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]].

questions.q: To stay under the 4,000-ft broken layer in Class E, what is the highest you may cruise, and what visibility do you need?
questions.a: 3,500 ft MSL, which keeps you 500 ft below the clouds, with at least 3 SM flight visibility below 10,000 MSL [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

questions.q: Visibility ahead drops to about 2 SM. Can you keep going VFR at 3,500?
questions.a: Not legally in Class E: you need 3 SM [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. It is also a risk signal. Don't continue VFR into IMC; wait it out or turn around [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

questions.q: Could you get into the destination Class D VFR, or another way?
questions.a: Not VFR: the ceiling is above 1,000 ft, but landing VFR needs 3 SM ground visibility [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]]. You could ask for special VFR: clear of clouds, 1 SM, before sunset needs no instrument rating [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]. You still need a safe route to the surface area.

questions.q: Why not just climb into the clouds and ask for an IFR clearance?
questions.a: You aren't instrument current, so you may not act as PIC under IFR [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]. Pilots whose skills have eroded can lose control in about 10 minutes on instruments [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. If it truly becomes an emergency, declare it and get ATC help [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]] [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]].

skills.do: Given an airspace class, MSL and AGL altitude, time of day and weather, say whether a VFR flight is legal, quote the 91.155, 91.157 or 91.159 line that decides it, and name a legal option (special VFR, a different altitude, a delay or IFR) when it isn't.
skills.practice: Before each flight, run the step-by-step questions for the departure, the en route altitude and the destination using the current METARs, and say the deciding rule out loud [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]] [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. For a flight review, the instructor should make sure you can comply with Part 91 in various airspace under a range of weather [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.1]], so drill the 91.155 table until you can recite it, then quiz yourself with the PHAK Figure 15-8 chart covered [[1:383|PHAK 15-8]].

quiz.q: You will fly VFR through Class C airspace. What does 91.155 require?
options: 3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
3 SM and clear of clouds
1 SM and clear of clouds
5 SM; 1,000 ft below and above, 1 SM horizontal
quiz.why: Class C uses 3 SM and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. Clear of clouds is Class B.

quiz.q: You level at exactly 1,200 ft AGL, the floor of the Class E above you. Which minimums apply?
options: Class E, because you are at its floor
Class G, the airspace below
Whichever is less restrictive
Special VFR minimums
quiz.why: At the base altitude of a Class E area you count as in the airspace directly below it [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]].

quiz.q: METAR at a Class D airport: SCT009 BKN014 OVC030, 5 SM. Does the 91.155(c) ceiling rule allow VFR beneath the ceiling?
options: No, the ceiling is 900 ft
No, any layer below 1,000 ft counts
Yes, the ceiling is 1,400 ft
Only with special VFR
quiz.why: The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, 1,400 ft; a scattered layer is not a ceiling [[60:3|14 CFR 1.1 Ceiling]]. That meets the 1,000-ft rule [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. You still must keep Class D cloud clearance from the scattered layer [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

quiz.q: Under special VFR in an airplane, what flight visibility do you need?
options: 1/2 SM
2 SM
3 SM
1 SM
quiz.why: Except for helicopters, SVFR needs at least 1 SM flight visibility [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

quiz.q: The sectional shows "NO SVFR" above an airport name. What does it mean?
options: SVFR is allowed only at night there
Fixed-wing special VFR is prohibited there
The airport has no weather reporting
SVFR needs a flight plan there
quiz.why: "NO SVFR" marks airports where fixed-wing SVFR is prohibited [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]], the Part 91 Appendix D, Section 3 list [[60:648|14 CFR Part 91 App. D, Sec. 3]].

quiz.q: Magnetic course 270°, cruising well above 3,000 ft AGL. Which altitude fits 91.159?
quiz.why: 180° through 359° uses even thousands + 500, such as 6,500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

quiz.q: Your magnetic course is 175°, but a crosswind gives a magnetic heading of 183°. Which rule picks your altitude?
options: Heading 183°: even + 500
Course 175°: odd + 500
Either, pilot's choice
True course, before variation
quiz.why: VFR cruising altitude goes by magnetic course (ground track) [[33:177|AIM 3-1-5, TBL 3-1-2]] [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: On an SVFR clearance, who is responsible for terrain and obstacle clearance?
options: The pilot
The controller, since you are on a clearance
The controller, only at radar facilities
Nobody; SVFR has no altitude
quiz.why: The clearance gives no specific altitude and the pilot is responsible for obstacle or terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, about how long does a pilot without instrument training, or with eroded skills, keep control once on instruments alone?
options: About 1 minute
About 10 minutes
About 30 minutes
Until fuel runs out, if trimmed
quiz.why: Accident statistics show these pilots lose control in about 10 minutes [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

takeaways: B: 3 SM, clear of clouds. C, D and E below 10,000 MSL: 3 SM, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 beside.
At or above 10,000 MSL (and more than 1,200 AGL in G): 5 SM, 1,000 above and below, 1 SM beside.
Class G at or below 1,200 AGL: 1 SM and clear of clouds by day only; night is 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000.
Surface areas: 1,000-ft ceiling to fly beneath, 3 SM ground visibility to take off, land or enter the pattern.
SVFR: clearance, clear of clouds, 1 SM, in surface areas only, sunrise to sunset unless instrument qualified and IFR-equipped.
Above 3,000 AGL: magnetic course 0-179 odd + 500, 180-359 even + 500.
Turn around early: continued VFR into IMC leads to loss of control and flight into terrain.
cfi_notes: Make the pilot work from the regulation text, not a memory aid. Many experienced pilots remember the table but forget 91.155(e), the base-of-Class-E rule [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]].
Probe the two "night" lines: 14 CFR 1.1 night (civil twilight) for the 91.155 table [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1 Night]] and sunset for fixed-wing SVFR [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]. Pilots often mix them.

91.157(c)(2) lets a part 91 pilot at a satellite airport with no weather reporting count cockpit visibility in takeoff position [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]]. Many pilots don't know it. The sources don't show when it was added, so don't teach a date.
AIM TBL 3-1-2 lists VFR flight levels above 18,000 ft; point out that Class A is IFR unless otherwise authorized [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]] and 91.159(b) says ATC-assigned [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(b)]].

The night SVFR text says "meets the applicable requirements for instrument flight under part 61" [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]; AIM 4-4-6g shortens it to "instrument rated" [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. Neither says whether 61.57(c) recency is included; treat that as an interpretation, check current FAA guidance, and note that being IFR current [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] meets either reading.

For R1, have the pilot set written personal minimums and a turn-back point before the flight [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]], and practice shallow (10° or less) turns by reference to instruments with a view-limiting device [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].
Part-time towers: have the pilot find the Chart Supplement "other times" line for the home airport [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].
gaps: The sources don't give sunrise, sunset or civil twilight times; pilots need an almanac or flight planning tool for the day and SVFR time limits.
Helicopter, powered parachute and weight-shift rules in 91.155 and 91.157, and the Alaska SVFR twilight rule, are left out (airplane only).
No source explains how each Class D or E surface area is charted locally, or which part-time towers revert to E or G; that is in each airport's Chart Supplement entry.

No source spells out which part 61 rules make up "the applicable requirements for instrument flight" for night SVFR; whether 61.57(c) recency is included is an interpretation the lesson flags, not teaches; confirm with current FAA guidance.

activities.title: Minimums by airspace class
activities.intro: Drag each set of VFR minimums to its numbered pin. Assume daytime. The 5 SM rule starts at 10,000 MSL, which this figure doesn't mark; every pin except the top two is below it.

pins.label: At or above 10,000 MSL: 5 SM; 1,000 above and below, 1 SM beside

activities.why: Class A is IFR [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]; Class B is 3 SM clear of clouds; Class D is 3 SM with 500/1,000/2,000; Class G at the surface by day is 1 SM clear of clouds; pin 5, Class E above 14,500 MSL, is above 10,000 MSL, so 5 SM and 1,000/1,000/1 SM [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. The 5 SM rule is not tied to 14,500: it applies at or above 10,000 MSL (and more than 1,200 ft AGL in Class G), so Class E from 10,000 to 14,500 needs it too [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

activities.title: How much visibility?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Special VFR in a Class D surface area

activities.why: Class G is 1 SM by day below 10,000 MSL and 3 SM at night; B, C, D and E below 10,000 are 3 SM; at or above 10,000 MSL (and more than 1,200 AGL in G) it is 5 SM [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. SVFR is 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

activities.title: Surface area and SVFR rules
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap the rule that applies.

pairs.r: No VFR beneath it; ask for special VFR
No VFR takeoff, landing or pattern entry
Use the minimums of the airspace below
Clear of clouds within 1/2 mile of the runway

pairs.l: SVFR takeoff, satellite field, no weather
pairs.r: Cockpit visibility in takeoff position may count

activities.title: Work out the legal altitude or time
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: True course 172°, variation 12° W. Highest terrain on the route is 2,000 ft MSL. What is the lowest cruising altitude that is more than 3,000 ft above that terrain and fits 91.159?
items.why: MC = 172 + 12 = 184° (west adds) [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. 184° needs even thousands + 500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. More than 3,000 ft above 2,000 MSL means above 5,000 MSL; 5,500 is odd, so 6,500.

items.q: Class E, below 10,000 MSL. A broken layer has its base at 4,500 ft MSL. What is the highest altitude you may cruise beneath it?
items.why: Class E below 10,000 MSL requires 500 ft below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]: 4,500 - 500 = 4,000 ft MSL.

items.q: Cloud tops are at 9,800 ft MSL in Class E. What is the lowest altitude you may fly directly above them?
items.why: Both Class E rows require 1,000 ft above clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]: 9,800 + 1,000 = 10,800 ft MSL. Up there you also need 5 SM.

items.q: Sunset is 1842 and evening civil twilight ends at 1910. You are en route (not in a traffic pattern) in Class G at 900 ft AGL with 1.5 SM visibility, clear of clouds. For how many minutes after sunset are you still legal?
items.why: Class G day minimums (1 SM, clear of clouds) apply until night, which starts at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1 Night]] [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. 1910 - 1842 = 28 minutes. At night you would need 3 SM.

activities.title: Can I legally go?
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a Cessna 172 without IFR equipment. You hold a private certificate, no instrument rating. You are at Hometown, a nontowered airport inside a Class E surface area. It is 1630; sunset is 1745. Hometown ASOS: wind calm, visibility 4 SM in mist, overcast 900 ft. Valley Airport, 25 NM away, reports 3,500 overcast and 10 SM.

steps.s: You want to fly to Valley. Can you take off VFR right now?
options: Yes: 4 SM is more than the 3 SM minimum
No: the ceiling is below 1,000 ft in a surface area, so you need special VFR or IFR
Yes, if you stay 500 ft below the clouds
No: special VFR needs 3 SM, so you can't go at all
steps.why: No VFR beneath a ceiling under 1,000 ft in a surface area, except under special VFR [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. SVFR needs only 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

steps.s: There is no tower at Hometown. Who do you ask for the SVFR clearance?
options: Nobody; announce it on the CTAF
The nearest tower, FSS or center
Only FSS, after filing a VFR flight plan
Any pilot on frequency
steps.why: In a Class E surface area, a clearance may be obtained from the nearest tower, FSS or center, and no complete flight plan is needed [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

steps.s: Cleared SVFR out of the surface area. Past the boundary you level at 600 ft AGL, under the 700-ft Class E floor, in Class G. Visibility 4 SM, clear of clouds. What now applies?
options: Still SVFR, with ATC separating you
Class G day: 1 SM and clear of clouds
3 SM and 500 ft below clouds
No minimums; Class G is uncontrolled
steps.why: SVFR is effective only inside the surface area [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. In Class G at or below 1,200 AGL by day, the rule is 1 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. You must still meet the 91.119 minimum safe altitudes [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

steps.s: Halfway, visibility drops to about 1 SM and the ridge ahead disappears into cloud. Valley still reports VFR. What do you do?
options: Follow the highway lower, under the clouds
Climb through the clouds to get on top
Make a shallow turn back toward better weather and ask ATC for help if needed
Descend to 300 ft AGL to see better
steps.why: Don't continue VFR into IMC; turn around [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. Scud running is a known pitfall [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. Keep turns to 10° of bank or less if visual references fade [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

steps.s: At 1735 you are back near Hometown, still 900 overcast. ATC says to expect a 20-minute delay for SVFR entry. What is your plan?
options: Hold and accept SVFR at 1755
Divert to an airport with VFR weather; after sunset you can't get SVFR
Enter VFR under the clouds; it is still twilight
Land anyway; the clearance is a formality
steps.why: Fixed-wing SVFR is only between sunrise and sunset unless the pilot meets the instrument requirements and the airplane is IFR-equipped [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. Diverting before you run low on options is the safe choice [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

activities.title: Old rules and myths
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: VFR cruising altitudes are chosen by magnetic heading.
cards.why: They are chosen by magnetic course (ground track) [[33:177|AIM 3-1-5, TBL 3-1-2]].

cards.s: 91.159 applies only in level cruise more than 3,000 ft above the surface.
cards.why: That is the rule's scope, with exceptions for short holding and turning [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]].

cards.s: You can ask for special VFR anywhere in Class E when the weather is low.
cards.why: SVFR exists only below 10,000 MSL within the lateral limits of a surface area [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(a)]].

cards.s: For fixed-wing SVFR without instrument qualifications, the time limit is sunset.
cards.why: 91.157(b)(4) says between sunrise and sunset [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

cards.s: Your own visibility estimate for an SVFR takeoff becomes an official ground visibility report.
cards.why: 91.157(d) says it is not an official weather or ground visibility report [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(d)]].

cards.s: Marginal VFR weather can still be legal VFR in Class E below 10,000 MSL.
cards.why: MVFR is 3 to 5 miles or 1,000 to 3,000 ft [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]]; Class E needs 3 SM and cloud clearance [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Day, Class E, 9,500 ft MSL, flight visibility 4 SM. A cloud base is 400 ft above you. Is the flight legal?
options: Yes, 4 SM exceeds the minimum
No, you need 500 ft below clouds
No, you need 5 SM at 9,500 ft
Yes, Class E only requires clear of clouds
final_quiz.why: Below 10,000 MSL in Class E: 3 SM and 500 ft below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. 400 ft is not enough.

final_quiz.q: You climb to 10,500 ft MSL in Class E with 4 SM visibility, well clear of clouds. Legal?
options: Yes, 3 SM is the Class E minimum
Yes, because you are clear of clouds
No, at or above 10,000 MSL you need 5 SM
No, VFR is not allowed above 10,000 ft
final_quiz.why: Class E at or above 10,000 MSL requires 5 SM [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Day, Class G, 2,000 ft AGL, 5,000 ft MSL, visibility 1.5 SM, clouds 600 ft above you. Legal?
options: No, Class G above 1,200 AGL needs 3 SM
No, you need 1,000 ft below clouds
Yes, if you stay within 1/2 mile of an airport
Yes, 1 SM and 500 ft below are met
final_quiz.why: Class G more than 1,200 AGL below 10,000 MSL by day: 1 SM, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You cruise at 3,500 ft MSL over the Class E surface area of an airport (elevation 500 ft) reporting 800 overcast, tops 2,000 ft MSL, with 5 SM below. Does 91.155(c) stop you?
options: No, it applies beneath the ceiling; you still need cloud clearance
Yes, no VFR anywhere in the surface area
Yes, unless you get special VFR
No, surface area rules apply only to towered airports
final_quiz.why: 91.155(c) bans VFR beneath a ceiling under 1,000 ft [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. Above, you are 1,500 ft over the tops, meeting the 1,000-ft-above rule [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You want to depart SVFR from a satellite airport with no weather reporting inside a Class D surface area. Part 91. How can the 1 SM be determined?
options: Only by a tower observer
By flight visibility, which may include what you see from the cockpit in takeoff position
By the nearest METAR within 25 NM
It can't; SVFR needs reported weather
final_quiz.why: 91.157(c)(2) lets flight visibility include cockpit visibility in takeoff position at such an airport [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]]; it is not an official report [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(d)]].

final_quiz.q: An instrument-rated, current pilot in an airplane equipped under 91.205(d) asks for SVFR at 2100. What does 91.157 say?
options: Not allowed; SVFR is day only for everyone
Allowed only with 3 SM visibility
Allowed, clear of clouds with 1 SM, if ATC issues the clearance
Allowed only at airports with a tower
final_quiz.why: The sunrise-to-sunset limit doesn't apply when the pilot meets the instrument requirements and the airplane has 91.205(d) equipment [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]] [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

final_quiz.q: You want SVFR into LaGuardia in a Cessna 172. What happens?
options: ATC issues it if traffic permits
Fixed-wing SVFR is prohibited there
It is allowed only before 0700
It needs a VFR flight plan
final_quiz.why: LaGuardia is on the Part 91 Appendix D, Section 3 list where fixed-wing SVFR is prohibited [[60:649|14 CFR Part 91 App. D, Sec. 3]].

final_quiz.q: Your SVFR clearance says "maintain special VFR conditions at or below 1,500." Terrain rises to 1,200 ft ahead. Who keeps you clear of it?
options: ATC, because it gave the altitude
You, the pilot
ATC, at radar facilities
Nobody, because 1,500 is above the terrain
final_quiz.why: ATC's altitude limit is for traffic; the pilot is responsible for obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: Magnetic course 359°, more than 3,000 ft AGL. Which altitude is correct?
final_quiz.why: 359° falls in 180° through 359°: even thousands + 500, such as 8,500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: The AIM table lists VFR flight levels like FL 195. Can you cruise VFR at FL 195 in the US?
options: Yes, on courses 0° to 179°
Yes, with a transponder
No, it is Class A, IFR unless otherwise authorized
No, VFR flight levels start at FL 300
final_quiz.why: Class A is 18,000 MSL to FL 600 and IFR unless otherwise authorized [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]; above 18,000 MSL fly what ATC assigns [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Approach control tells you to "maintain VFR at 5,000" on a magnetic course of 090°, 4,000 ft AGL. What do you do?
options: Climb to 5,500 to comply with 91.159
Refuse: 5,000 is not a VFR altitude
Descend below 3,000 AGL
Fly 5,000; 91.159 applies unless ATC authorizes otherwise
final_quiz.why: 91.159 applies "unless otherwise authorized by ATC" [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]].

final_quiz.q: Stations along your route report VFR near minimums, temperature-dewpoint spread 2 °C. What does AC 91-92 warn?
options: Areas between stations may be below VFR, and fog may form
Reports near minimums mean the route is VFR
Only visibility matters, not the spread
Climb on top and look for a hole later
final_quiz.why: AC 91-92 warns that areas en route may be below VFR, fog may form at a spread of 3 °C or less, and not to go on top hoping for a hole [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

final_quiz.q: You blunder into cloud VFR, not instrument current. Per the AFH, how should you turn back?
options: 30° bank to get out fast
Standard-rate with a descent
Shallow, no more than 10° of bank, wings level between turns
Don't turn; climb until on top
final_quiz.why: Use the smallest practical bank, no more than 10°, and avoid combined maneuvers [[24:368|AFH 18-19]] [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

final_quiz.q: METAR: 2,500 broken, 4 SM. Your flight is in Class E below 10,000 MSL. Which is true?
options: It is MVFR and not legal VFR
It is IFR; you need a clearance
It is MVFR but can be legal VFR with 500 ft below clouds
It is VFR with no limits
final_quiz.why: Ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 or visibility 3 to 5 is MVFR [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]]. Class E below 10,000 needs 3 SM and 500 below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].
